readerTitle: The hire everyone liked, and the gap nobody saw
caseNote: 가상 사례 (비스트로 주방, 소프트웨어 스타트업) + 실제 연구 (Lauren Rivera의 엘리트 전문서비스 기업 채용 연구)
insight: 문화를 '함께 지키는 원칙'과 '스타일·배경'으로 나누면, 원칙은 같은 사람을, 스타일은 팀에 없는 사람을 찾게 된다.
misconception: '우리 팀과 잘 맞는 사람'을 뽑으면 문화가 지켜진다. 실제로는 '나와 비슷한 사람'을 뽑아 팀의 빈틈을 키우기 쉽다.

sources.text: Rivera, L. A. (2012). Hiring as Cultural Matching: The Case of Elite Professional Service Firms. American Sociological Review, 77(6).
Rivera, L. A. (2015). Pedigree: How Elite Students Get Elite Jobs. Princeton University Press.
주방과 스타트업 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Rivera(2012)는 투자은행·컨설팅·로펌 채용 담당자들이 여가 활동, 경험, 자기표현 방식의 유사성을 '핏'의 근거로 삼았다고 보고합니다. 카드 5에는 수치 없이 일반적으로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 논문 원문으로 표현을 확인하세요.
'공항에 함께 갇혀도 괜찮을 사람' 류의 기준이 Rivera의 인터뷰 자료에 등장하는지 원문(2012 논문 또는 Pedigree)에서 확인하세요. 확인되지 않으면 카드 5의 해당 문장을 삭제합니다.
'culture add'라는 용어는 특정 연구가 아니라 실무에서 널리 쓰이는 표현입니다. 카드에서 연구 결과로 제시하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The hire everyone liked, and the gap nobody saw
body: A small bistro's kitchen runs like a family. Same jokes, same playlist, same love of improvising a special at 6 p.m.
Every new cook was hired because the team said, "They'll fit right in." They always did. And every Saturday, the kitchen still fell apart in the same way.

image.label: Five cooks in matching style laughing in a busy kitchen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 비스트로 주방에서 비슷한 두건과 앞치마를 한 요리사 다섯 명이 웃고 있음. 뒤편 주문표 레일에는 주문서가 넘치게 쌓여 있음. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Two sous chef candidates. Both cook well.
body: Candidate one trained at the same school as your head chef, loves the same music, and had the team laughing during the trial shift.
Candidate two came from a busy hotel banquet kitchen. Quieter. She ran the trial shift off a written prep list and questioned one of your steps. Both are honest and reliable. Who do you hire?

options.text: Candidate one. The team already clicks with him
options.feedback: You get an easy first month. But you add a second copy of what the kitchen already has, and the Saturday problem stays.

options.text: Candidate two. She brings the structure the kitchen lacks
options.feedback: She shares the values that matter and brings a skill nobody has. The cost is some friction while the team adjusts.
Involving the team builds buy-in. But a vote usually rewards whoever felt most familiar, which is candidate one.

cards.title: The kitchen kept hiring itself.
body: Each cook was great at creativity and speed. Nobody liked lists, ordering or costing. So food costs drifted and Saturdays ran on adrenaline.

"Fit" was doing quiet work in every interview. It didn't mean *shares our standards*. It meant **feels like us**. A team that hires for that gets stronger at what it already does well, and blinder to what it doesn't.

cards.title: Culture fit vs culture add
body: **Culture fit** asks: is this person like us? **Culture add** asks: does this person share what we stand for, and bring something we're missing?
The difference is what gets compared. Fit often compares personality, background and taste. Add compares values first, then looks for the gaps.

image.label: Two-layer diagram: shared core, different edges
image.brief: 두 겹 원 인포그래픽. 안쪽 원 "Must match: values, standards"는 모두 같은 색. 바깥 고리 "Look for gaps: skills, experience, style"는 사람마다 다른 색 조각. 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: "Fit" often means "similar to me."
body: Sociologist Lauren Rivera studied hiring at elite banks, consulting firms and law firms. She found that many interviewers treated fit as a major criterion, and judged it largely by shared hobbies, experiences and ways of presenting oneself.

Some interviewers framed it as whether they'd enjoy being stuck with the candidate on a long trip. That feels like judging teamwork. It's mostly judging **similarity**, which says little about how someone will do the job.

cards.title: Split culture into two layers before you interview.
body: Write both down before you meet anyone:
list: **Must match:** how we treat customers, honesty, reliability, how we handle mistakes
**Look for gaps:** skills, work experience, thinking style, background
Then ask in every interview: *what would this person do that nobody here does now?*
cards.callout: If you can't name the gap, you're probably hiring for similarity.
cards.softwareNote: In a small software team, the gap is often a missing perspective: someone who has done customer support, sold the product, or worked in the industry your users come from.

cards.title: Difference has costs, and limits.
body: Culture add is not "anyone different will do." If someone doesn't share the must-match values, the difference will hurt, not help.

Difference also brings friction. A newcomer who questions every habit can be worn down or pushed out if the manager doesn't make room for her. And "culture add" can become just another gut label. Write the gap down, or the old bias returns under a new name.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: Your six engineers all came from large tech companies. They build polished features, but users keep churning because onboarding confuses them.
You're hiring engineer seven. Which approach fits this lesson best?

options.text: Hire another big-tech engineer the team vouches for
options.feedback: Fast ramp-up and easy trust. But you deepen the same blind spot that's costing you users.

options.text: Define must-match values, then favor a candidate who has worked closely with confused users, like a former support engineer
options.feedback: You protect the shared standards and fill the gap behind the churn. Expect some debates about priorities at first.

options.text: Hire whoever is most different from the current team
options.feedback: Right instinct, wrong target. Difference only helps when it fills a real gap and the values still match.

cards.title: Match on values. Hire for the gap.
body: "Fits in" often means "reminds us of us." Decide what must be shared, then look for what's missing.
**Try it today:** write three must-match values for your team, and one thing nobody on the team is good at. That second line is your next hire's job.
